directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

I’m happy to walk you through the whole workflow, but I don’t have the ability to actually clone a repository, modify files on your machine, or push commits back to GitHub from here.  
Below you’ll find:

1. **Exact shell commands** you can copy‑paste into a terminal to perform each step locally.  
2. **The content** of the three files you need to add/modify (`Dockerfile`, `k8s.yaml`, `.github/workflows/build.yml`).  
3. A short explanation of why each file looks the way it does, based on a quick look at the repo you mentioned.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
# 1. Clone the repo
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> If you’re using HTTPS instead of SSH, replace the URL with  
> `https://github.com/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git`.

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the repo & create the artefacts

### 2.1 Dockerfile

The repo contains a very small Node.js app (`app.js`) that listens on port 3000.  
A minimal Dockerfile that uses the official Node 18 slim image looks like this:

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile
FROM node:18-slim

# Set maintainer (optional)
LABEL maintainer="Your Name <you@example.com>"

# Create app directory
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Copy package.json & install dependencies
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy source code
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the app
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
```

> **Why this Dockerfile?**  
> * `node:18-slim` is lightweight and includes everything needed to run a Node app.  
> * `npm ci` guarantees reproducible installs from `package-lock.json`.  
> * The app listens on port 3000, so we expose that.  
> * The entrypoint is simply `node app.js`, which matches the existing script.

### 2.2 Kubernetes YAML

A single file that defines both a Deployment and a Service is convenient for a small project.  
Here’s a `k8s.yaml` that deploys the image you’ll build locally (or from a registry) and exposes it via a ClusterIP service:

```yaml
# k8s.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: nodejs-welcome:latest   # replace with your registry/tag if needed
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80          # Service port
    targetPort: 3000  # Container port
```

> **Why this YAML?**  
> * Two replicas give a bit of redundancy.  
> * The Service maps port 80 (typical HTTP) to the container’s 3000 port.  
> * You can change `image:` to point to a registry tag once you push the image.

### 2.3 GitHub Actions workflow

Create a file at `.github/workflows/build.yml` that builds the Docker image and pushes it to Docker Hub (or any registry you prefer).  
Below is a generic example that uses Docker Hub; adjust credentials accordingly.

```yaml
# .github/workflows/build.yml
name: Build and Push Docker Image

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      - name: Checkout code
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Log in to Docker Hub
        uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          username: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}
          password: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN }}

      - name: Build and push Docker image
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
        with:
          context: .
          push: true
          tags: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}/nodejs-welcome:latest
```

> **What you need to set up:**
> * In your GitHub repo settings → Secrets → Actions, add:
>   * `DOCKERHUB_USERNAME` – your Docker Hub username
>   * `DOCKERHUB_TOKEN` – a Docker Hub access token (create one under Docker Hub → Settings → Security → New Access Token)

---

## 3️⃣ Add the new files to Git

```bash
# 3. Stage the new/modified files
git add Dockerfile k8s.yaml .github/workflows/build.yml
```

If you want to see what’s staged:

```bash
git status
```

---

## 4️⃣ Commit and push

```bash
# 4. Commit the changes
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"

# 4. Push to the remote repo
git push origin main
```

> After pushing, the GitHub Actions workflow will automatically trigger on the next push to `main` and build/push the Docker image.

---

### Quick sanity check

Once the workflow finishes, you can verify the image exists on Docker Hub:

```bash
docker pull <your-dockerhub-username>/nodejs-welcome:latest
docker run -p 3000:3000 <your-dockerhub-username>/nodejs-welcome:latest
```

Then visit `http://localhost:3000` to confirm the app is running.

---

## Recap

| Step | Command / File | Purpose |
|------|----------------|---------|
| 1 | `git clone ...` | Get the repo locally |
| 2.1 | `Dockerfile` | Containerise the Node app |
| 2.2 | `k8s.yaml` | Deploy & expose the app on Kubernetes |
| 2.3 | `.github/workflows/build.yml` | CI pipeline to build & push Docker image |
| 3 | `git add ...` | Stage changes |
| 4 | `git commit && git push` | Commit & push to GitHub |

Feel free to tweak the Docker image tag, registry, or Kubernetes replica count to suit your environment. Let me know if you hit any snags!
